clinicalPearls: Typically affects older adults and reflects degenerative narrowing of the central canal, lateral recesses, or neural foramina
The hallmark symptom is neurogenic claudication: bilateral buttock, thigh, and calf discomfort, heaviness, or paraesthesiae brought on by standing and walking
Symptoms are characteristically relieved by lumbar flexion, such as sitting, leaning forward on a shopping trolley, or cycling, because flexion enlarges the canal
Walking downhill (which extends the spine) tends to worsen symptoms whereas bending forward or walking uphill eases them, a useful contrast with vascular claudication
Vascular claudication is relieved simply by stopping and standing still and is associated with diminished peripheral pulses, unlike neurogenic claudication which requires postural flexion for relief
Neurological examination is often normal at rest, and deficits may only emerge after a provocative period of walking
MRI is the investigation of choice, and standing or extension imaging can reveal dynamic compression not apparent when supine
Initial management is conservative (activity modification, physiotherapy, analgesia, epidural steroid injection); decompressive surgery is considered for disabling or progressive symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Lumbar spinal stenosis arises from progressive degenerative narrowing of the spinal canal and its lateral recesses and neural foramina. A combination of intervertebral disc bulging, facet joint hypertrophy, thickening and buckling of the ligamentum flavum, and sometimes degenerative spondylolisthesis reduces the space available for the cauda equina and exiting nerve roots. The compression is dynamic: spinal extension during standing and walking further narrows the canal and compromises neural blood flow, producing the characteristic exertional leg symptoms, whereas flexion enlarges the canal and relieves them. Venous congestion and transient ischaemia of the compressed nerve roots are thought to underlie the claudicant pattern.
additionalDifferentials: Vascular (arterial) claudication from peripheral arterial disease
Trochanteric bursitis or other referred hip pathology
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the lumbar spine as the investigation of choice
Standing and flexion-extension radiographs to assess instability or degenerative spondylolisthesis
CT or CT myelography where MRI is contraindicated
Ankle-brachial pressure index and vascular studies to exclude arterial claudication
Nerve conduction studies and EMG if peripheral neuropathy is suspected
redFlags: New saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or incontinence, or faecal incontinence suggesting cauda equina syndrome and mandating urgent MRI
Constitutional features such as weight loss, fever, or night pain suggesting malignancy or infection
reference.prognosis: Many patients have a stable or slowly progressive course and can be managed conservatively for years; decompressive surgery gives good relief of leg symptoms in appropriately selected patients, although back pain and other degenerative changes may persist.
pitfalls: Mistaking neurogenic for vascular claudication, or vice versa, and instituting the wrong management
Attributing symptoms to imaging findings when incidental degenerative narrowing is common in the asymptomatic elderly
Overlooking coexisting hip osteoarthritis as a cause of buttock and leg pain
Missing an evolving cauda equina syndrome
references: North American Spine Society Clinical Guidelines: Degenerative Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
management: Manage conservatively first with flexion-based physiotherapy and exercise, activity modification and simple analgesia, since the course is often stable or slowly progressive
Trial neuropathic analgesics for leg symptoms, recognising the limited evidence in neurogenic claudication
Offer an epidural corticosteroid injection for symptom relief in patients unsuitable for or awaiting surgery
Refer for decompressive surgery such as laminectomy when neurogenic claudication is disabling or refractory to conservative care
Add instrumented fusion where there is associated degenerative spondylolisthesis or instability
Exclude vascular claudication with ankle-brachial pressure index and peripheral pulse assessment before attributing symptoms to stenosis
Escalate urgently for a progressive neurological deficit or features of cauda equina syndrome
